\title{Counting Collapse in Autoregressive Text-to-Speech:\\
       A Lean-Verified Bound, and a Horizon It Does Not Yet Explain}

\twoauthors
  {Ivan Viakhirev$^{1}$, Kirill Borodin$^{2,3}$, Grach Mkrtchian$^{2}$}
  {$^{1}$ITMO University, Russia \\
   $^{2}$lab260, Moscow Technical University of Communications and Informatics, Russia \\
   $^{3}$BitmanagerAI, UAE}
  {}{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Autoregressive text-to-speech models loop, truncate, and lose count on text that
repeats a phrase many times. Modelling one repetition as a state map $F$ on the
decoder's hidden state, we prove that if $F$ contracts with factor $q<1$ then
\emph{no} Lipschitz readout---the model's own stop head included---can separate
repetition counts beyond a horizon $N^\ast \le \log(\mu/(2LC))/\log q$. Both it and a
companion dilution lemma are machine-checked in Lean~4 with \texttt{mathlib},
free of \texttt{sorry} and nonstandard axioms. We do \emph{not} establish the theorem's premise: two
attempts to measure the contraction factor failed and the dilution lemma's dose-response test came
out sign-reversed. Across
\NModels{} checkpoints from \NFamilies{} architectures, judged by a CTC recogniser, the
obvious autoregressive judge being biased against repetition,
models render repeated text with a median count error of \ErrRepCk{}\% per
checkpoint at $k\ge6$
and are exact in \ExactRep{}\% of generations, against \ExactCtl{}\% for
length-matched \emph{distinct}-word controls: the limit tracks periodicity, not
length, in every checkpoint and family ($n{=}6$, too small to test). It may not
be peculiar to autoregressive decoding: of two non-autoregressive baselines, one
is immune and one is not. Up to $k=32$ the count stays proportional rather than saturating, so
no horizon is visible there; a post-hoc and exploratory extension to $k=128$ finds
one, repetition lowering the fitted saturation scale \HzFormLo{}--\HzFormHi{}-fold
by fitted family, though not in
one of the \HzNModels{} checkpoints that can utter that much. Its \emph{conclusion} survives one
direct test --- a linear readout recovers the count from decoder states below the
horizon and no better than chance past it --- in \PhNLost{} of the \PhNCk{}
checkpoints we could run it on.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
speech synthesis, hallucination, autoregressive models, formal verification,
fixed-point dynamics
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ask an autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) model to say \emph{six hundred
sixty-six thousand six hundred sixty-six}, or to repeat a word a dozen times, and
it will frequently get the count wrong: it stops early, runs on, or locks into a
loop. The behaviour is documented as a stability
problem~\cite{song2024ellav,wang2023valle} and usually attributed to
exposure bias or to the absence of a monotonic alignment constraint, with fixes
proposed at the level of attention supervision or decoding
rules~\cite{xin2024ralle,du2024cosyvoice2} --- the speech analogue of neural text
degeneration, whose remedies are likewise sampling- or
objective-level~\cite{holtzman2020curious,welleck2020neural}.

We argue that much of this behaviour has a simpler cause, statable as a theorem.
When the conditioning text contains $k$ copies of one phrase, softmax attention
cannot tell one copy from another: each gets weight $\Theta(1/k)$ and the profile
flattens (Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}). The decoder therefore meets approximately
the \emph{same} conditioning at every repetition boundary, so the map between
boundaries is approximately autonomous. If that map contracts, its record of how
many repetitions it has produced is erased geometrically, and past a computable
horizon no Lipschitz function of the state---the stop-token logit included---can
recover the count (Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}).

The failure is thus predicted to depend on \emph{periodicity}, not on length: a
sequence of $k$ distinct words should survive where $k$ identical ones do not.
That contrast is the sharpest test we run.

We contribute a conditional impossibility result for repetition counting in AR
decoders, its horizon explicit in the contraction factor, orbit scale and readout
margin --- explicit as a formula, since we never measure those quantities for any
checkpoint; an elementary machine-checked proof of it and of the
attention-dilution lemma, in Lean~4 over \texttt{mathlib} with a reproducible
axiom audit --- to our knowledge the first hallucination result in speech
synthesis carried out as a formal artifact; and a parametric repetition-ladder benchmark with matched
controls and a non-autoregressive baseline. The work is the autoregressive-decoder companion to a
spectral study of hallucination in encoder--decoder
ASR~\cite{viakhirev2026dispersion}, which identified an attractor regime
descriptively; here the attractor is what the theorem is about.

\section{Counting Collapse}
\label{sec:theory}

Let $S$ be the decoder state space, a nonempty complete metric space ($\mathbb{R}^d$
in practice). Fix a prompt containing $k$ copies of a phrase and write
$s_m \in S$ for the state at the $m$-th \emph{repetition boundary}, after $m$
copies have been rendered.

\begin{assumption}[Periodic conditioning]\label{ass:periodic}
There is a single map $F : S \to S$ with $s_{m+1} = F(s_m)$ for all $m$.
\end{assumption}

This is what the lemma buys: if the decoder cannot distinguish the $k$ spans, its
update between consecutive boundaries is the same to within $O(\delta + 1/k)$.

\begin{lemma}[Attention dilution]\label{lem:dilution}
Let $z_1,\dots,z_k$ be attention logits over the $k$ repeated spans with
$z_a - z_b \le \delta$ for all $a,b$. Then
$e^{-\delta}/k \le \mathrm{softmax}(z)_i \le e^{\delta}/k$ for every $i$, hence
$|\mathrm{softmax}(z)_i - \mathrm{softmax}(z)_j| \le (e^\delta-e^{-\delta})/k$,
and the profile entropy satisfies $H \ge \log k - \delta$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{assumption}[Contraction]\label{ass:contraction}
$F$ is $q$-Lipschitz with $q < 1$.
\end{assumption}

Assumption~\ref{ass:contraction} is an empirical claim about a particular
decoder, not a theorem about transformers; where it fails, so is the bound. Write
$C = d(s_0, F s_0)/(1-q)$ for the orbit scale.

\begin{theorem}[Counting collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:periodic} and~\ref{ass:contraction}: (i)
$d(s_m, s^\ast) \le C q^m$ for the unique fixed point $s^\ast$; (ii) for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(s_m,s_n)<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n \ge N$;
(iii) every $L$-Lipschitz readout $g$ satisfies
$|g(s_m)-g(s_n)| \le LC(q^m+q^n)$; and therefore (iv) if $g$ still separates
counts $m \le n$ with decision margin $\mu>0$, then $\mu \le 2LCq^m$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizon}
  m \;\le\; \log\!\big(\mu / (2LC)\big)\big/\log q \;=:\; N^\ast .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

Part~(iv) is the operative statement: how many repetitions a decoder can count is
bounded by how fast its per-repetition map contracts, how large its orbit is, and
how much separation its readout needs. No property of the decoding rule enters,
so the bound covers greedy, sampled and beam decoding alike.

\noindent\textbf{Formal verification.}
Both results are formalised in Lean~4 against \texttt{mathlib}: part~(i)
specialises its Banach fixed-point machinery, while (ii)--(iv) and all of
Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} are proved from scratch. The development contains no
\texttt{sorry}, and an axiom audit confirms every exported theorem depends only
on \texttt{propext}, \texttt{Classical.choice} and \texttt{Quot.sound}.
Formalisation also forced the separation between what is proved (the implication)
and what is measured (the premise).

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\noindent\textbf{Stimuli.}
A parametric repetition ladder of \NStimuli{} items: carrier sentences with a
target word repeated $k \in \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,32\}$ times, plus repeated
sentences, tongue twisters, and English number phrases with intrinsic digit-word
repetition. Every word- and sentence-repetition item at $k\ge2$ has a
\emph{length-matched control}: same carrier and word count, the repeated token
replaced by fillers from a per-template pool of eight, cycled above $k\!=\!8$
(S10).

\noindent\textbf{Models.}
\NModels{} checkpoints but only \NFamilies{} designs, scale variants making up
the difference: Llasa at 1B/3B/8B (Llama backbones over X-codec2
tokens~\cite{ye2025llasa}) and Qwen3-TTS at 0.6B/1.7B are within-architecture
ladders, plus XTTS-v2~\cite{casanova2024xtts}; every checkpoint renders every
item at \NSeeds{} seeds. VITS~\cite{kim2021vits} and
F5-TTS~\cite{chen2024f5tts} are run as non-autoregressive baselines at the same
\NSeeds{} seeds, and XTTS-v2 and Qwen3-TTS-0.6B at altered repetition penalty as
ablations; none is pooled into the panel.

\noindent\textbf{Behavioural measurement, and why the obvious judge is wrong.}
The natural instrument, Whisper large-v3~\cite{radford2023whisper}, is
demonstrably the wrong one: its decoder is autoregressive with a language-model
prior, so it is subject to the very dynamics under study. Audited against
concatenative audio with known ground truth its counted/true ratio falls to
$0.27$--$0.65$ for $k\ge4$, while \emph{same-voice distinct-word} sequences of
identical length score $1.00$ --- a bias specific to periodicity, pointing the
way of the effect we want to measure. We score instead with a CTC recogniser
(\texttt{wav2vec2-large-960h-lv60-self}): no decoder, no language model, output
length governed by the acoustics. Worse in absolute WER, right for this purpose,
and put through the same audit: ratio \CtcValPer{} on periodic ground truth
against \WhisperValPer{} for Whisper. Both transcript sets are released.

The reported quantity is the \emph{relative count error} $(\hat c - k)/k$ for
$\hat c$ units delivered; exact-match scores $30$-of-$32$ and $3$-of-$32$ alike.
Audio-level degeneracy is detected separately.
Of \MainNGen{} panel generations we exclude \MainExclTmpl{} in one template
whose fillers the judge never transcribes, \MainExclCap{} stopped by our token
budget rather than by the model, and \MainExclDegen{} degenerate, leaving
\MainKept{}; per-condition rates are in S10, where the template rule falls evenly
on both arms and the budget rule works against the contrast.

\noindent\textbf{State measurement.}
For each instrumented generation we record per-step hidden states at probe layers
and head-averaged attention onto the text span, reporting the trajectory's
effective rank against $k$.

\noindent\textbf{Code, data, settings.}
Lean development, stimuli, code, per-item tables and both transcript sets are on
branch \texttt{research/ar-tts-counting-collapse} of
\url{https://github.com/lab260ru/icassp_antispoofing} (name predates this study).
\texttt{build.sh} regenerates every number here from pinned revisions (S19), and
a stratified
\SampleN{}-clip sample spanning every model, $k$ band and outcome ships with each
clip's transcript and scoring decision, so a judgement can be checked by ear. Full audio and activations regenerate from the
released seeds. Sampling uses shipped defaults
(XTTS-v2 $T{=}0.75$/$0.85$/$50$/penalty $5.0$; Llasa $T{=}0.8$, top-$p$ $1.0$;
Qwen3-TTS $T{=}0.9$/$1.0$/$50$/$1.05$), making Qwen3-TTS the \emph{most}
stochastic family, so its larger checkpoint's null is not an artifact of
conservative decoding. The penalty is the one parameter we vary.
